children: Calls for a U.S. ban on diesel exports are gaining momentum as retail prices reach record highs, with prolonged disruptions to Middle East and Russian refineries continuing to tighten global supplies ahead of winter, but some analysts cautioned that a ban would only offer short-term benefits for some Americans while causing harm to others.

The national average retail diesel price reached $6.51/gal on Monday, the highest on record, according to AAA, compared to a year ago, when prices averaged $3.695/gal; states with the highest diesel prices include California at $8.42/gal, Washington at $7.44/gal, and Hawaii at $7.18/gal.
President Trump has blamed the record diesel prices largely on Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, but the U.S. war with Iran has also pushed prices higher.

Meanwhile, Iowa Republican Senator Grassley has called on the Trump administration to ban U.S. diesel exports in an effort to ease prices for American farmers and truckers, and other vulnerable Republicans from Midwest states followed suit.
The idea of an export ban reportedly has not gained traction in the Trump administration, at least for now.
Analysts and oil executives say curtailments could have unintended consequences that would likely end up increasing prices domestically.

Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas official Garret Golding wrote on X that a diesel export ban could initially help lower wholesale prices in the U.S., especially on the Gulf Coast, but such a move also would reduce global supply, pushing diesel and distillate prices higher, and backfire on portions of the U.S. that rely on imports, such as the East Coast.
Refineries that could no longer export diesel would quickly run out of storage space and be forced to reduce their run rates, Golding noted.

When "you reduce run rates because you can't export distillate/diesel, you end up reducing how much gasoline, jet fuel, and other refined products you're producing, which means higher prices," Golding wrote.

On Monday, crude oil futures extended their slide to four sessions on easing concerns about oil flows out of the Middle East and expectations for renewed diplomatic efforts to bring the U.S. and Iran back to the negotiating table.

"Crude oil is tanking on the possibility that President Trump and Iranian President Pezeshkian could meet at the United Nations as early as tomorrow," Mizuho commodity specialist Robert Yawger said in a note, adding that the chances of a deal are "better than they were at the end of last week."
